title: Orata al Cartoccio
subtitle: sea bream baked in a parcel with olives, capers, and tomatoes
excerpt: Orata al cartoccio bakes sea bream fillets or a whole fish inside a sealed parchment parcel with cherry tomatoes, olives, capers, and white wine. The fish steams in its own juices and the tomato liquid forms a ready-made sauce. Serves 2.
sourceNotes: Cooking en papillote (al cartoccio in Italian) is a standard technique of the Italian and French Mediterranean kitchen. The cartoccio (paper bag or parchment parcel) creates a sealed environment in which the fish steams in its own liquid alongside whatever aromatics and vegetables are included. Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina (1891, public domain in Italy), gives a recipe for fish al cartoccio. The combination of sea bream (orata, Sparus aurata) with cherry tomatoes, Sicilian capers, black olives, and white wine is characteristic of southern Italian coastal cooking and appears in cookbooks from Campania, Sicily, and Puglia.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble the parcels up to 2 hours ahead and refrigerate until ready to bake.

glossaryTerms.definition: Cooked in a sealed parcel of baking parchment or foil. The parcel traps steam and creates a humid cooking environment that keeps fish moist and allows the flavours of the vegetables and aromatics to infuse the fish as it cooks. The parcel is opened at the table.

content.text: is the most forgiving way to cook fish. The sealed parchment parcel keeps in all the moisture, and the combination of cherry tomatoes, olives, capers, and white wine creates a cooking liquid that becomes a ready-made sauce as the fish bakes. There is almost no way to dry out the fish because the steam inside the parcel compensates for any loss of moisture from the flesh.

The parcels can be made with baking parchment or foil. Parchment can be folded and crimped to seal; foil can be sealed by folding the edges tightly. The parcels must be airtight: any gap lets steam escape and the method fails. Open at the table: the steam that billows out as you cut the parcels open is part of the experience.

items.prepNote: 2 sea bream fillets (about 200g each), skin on

content.text: Heat the oven to 200°C fan (220°C conventional). Cut two large sheets of baking parchment, each big enough to fold over and seal around a fish fillet with a generous margin.

Lay each fish fillet skin-side down in the centre of a parchment sheet. Distribute {{cherry-tomatoes}} of cherry tomatoes, {{olives-black}} of olives, {{capers}} of capers, and {{garlic}} of garlic slices equally between the two parcels. Add thyme sprigs if using. Drizzle with {{olive-oil}} of olive oil. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt and {{black-pepper}} of black pepper. Pour {{dry-white-wine}} of white wine over each parcel (40 ml per parcel).
Fold the parchment over the fish and crimp the edges tightly to seal, making a half-moon shape. Place on a baking tray.

Bake for 15 to 18 minutes until the parcels have puffed and the fish is cooked through. Place the unopened parcels on warm plates and take to the table. Snip or tear open at the table. Finish with {{parsley-flat}} of parsley and lemon wedges.

items.cause: Parcel not fully sealed, or fish cooked for too long
items.fix: Seal the parcel tightly with no gaps. Reduce baking time for thinner fillets. A 2 cm thick fillet takes 15 minutes.

items.symptom: Liquid in the parcel tastes watery rather than saucy
items.cause: Not enough tomatoes, or wine proportion too high
items.fix: Add more cherry tomatoes. They provide the body; wine alone is thin.

content.text: Orata (sea bream, Sparus aurata) is the premium fish of southern Italian coastal cooking. It is farmed along the coasts of Puglia, Campania, and Sicily in large quantities and appears on Italian restaurant menus year-round. Al cartoccio is one of the most common preparations: it requires almost no skill, produces excellent results, and allows the cook to plate straight from the parcel. In coastal trattorie the parcels arrive sealed and are opened at the table, which is both theatrical and practical. The liquid that pours out when the parcel is cut is the sauce; it goes onto the fish or is soaked up with good bread.
